tells.name: “delve” and kin
tells.what: The first famous tell. “Delve into”, “delves”, “delving”.
tells.fix: Say what you will do (“look at”, “compare”, “list”).

examples.bad: Let’s delve into the data.
examples.good: Here’s what the data shows.

tells.name: “tapestry”, “testament to”, “realm”
tells.what: Ornate nouns used as filler metaphors.

detect.pattern: \b(?:rich |intricate |vibrant )?tapestry\b|\ba testament to\b|\brealm of\b|\btreasure trove\b|\bbeacon of\b|\bsymphony of\b

tells.fix: Name the things the metaphor stands in for.

examples.bad: a rich tapestry of cultures
examples.good: Greek, Turkish and Armenian families on one street

tells.name: “landscape”, “ever-evolving”, “in today’s world”
tells.what: Openers that place the topic in a vague, shifting world.
tells.fix: Start with the specific fact.

examples.bad: In today’s fast-paced digital landscape, teams need speed.
examples.good: Our deploys take 40 minutes.

tells.name: “underscores”, “showcasing”, “pivotal”, “crucial”
tells.what: Academic-sounding verbs and adjectives of emphasis.
tells.fix: Cut the emphasis word and state the fact.

examples.bad: This underscores the pivotal role of caching.
examples.good: Caching cut p95 latency from 800ms to 90ms.

tells.name: “It’s important to note”, “It’s worth noting”
tells.what: Throat-clearing before a point.

detect.pattern: \bit(?:'|’)?s (?:important|worth|crucial|essential) (?:to note|noting|to remember|mentioning|to understand)\b|\bit is (?:important|worth|crucial|essential) (?:to note|noting|to remember|mentioning|to understand)\b

tells.fix: Delete the preamble. The point stands without it.

examples.bad: It’s important to note that the API has a rate limit.
examples.good: The API allows 100 calls a minute.

tells.name: “As an AI language model”
tells.what: Model names itself to hedge or refuse.

detect.pattern: \bas an ai(?: language model| assistant)?\b|\bmy (?:training data|knowledge cutoff)\b

tells.fix: Drop it. Answer, or say plainly what you can’t do.

examples.bad: As an AI language model, I don’t have personal opinions, but...
examples.good: Most reviewers prefer the second draft.

tells.name: “streamline”, “unlock”, “elevate”, “leverage”, “foster”
tells.what: Pitch-deck verbs where nobody is pitching.
tells.fix: Use the plain verb (“use”, “speed up”, “let you”, “help”).

examples.bad: Our new dashboard empowers teams to unlock insights and elevate their workflow.
examples.good: The dashboard shows which tests fail most often.

tells.name: “robust”, “holistic”, “nuanced”, “comprehensive”
tells.what: Abstract quality adjectives that sound careful and say little.
tells.fix: Name the property (“handles 10k req/s”, “covers all 50 states”).

examples.bad: We built a robust, holistic, scalable framework for data quality.
examples.good: We check every row for nulls and bad dates before it loads.

tells.name: “journey”, “embark”, “navigate”, “bustling”, “nestled”
tells.what: Travel and scenery words used for things that are not trips or places.
tells.fix: Name the task or the place.

examples.bad: Embark on a journey through the landscape of modern databases.
examples.good: This post compares Postgres and SQLite for small apps.

tells.name: “genuinely”, “a genuine”, “is a genuinely”
tells.what: Sincerity markers. The current Claude tell, the way “delve” was GPT’s.
tells.fix: Delete it. If the claim needs it to be believed, add evidence instead.

examples.bad: This is a genuinely useful tool.
examples.good: This tool saved us a day per release.

tells.name: “That distinction matters”, “Why X matters”
tells.what: Announces that something is important instead of showing the stakes.
tells.fix: Show what goes wrong without it. Readers will see that it matters.

examples.bad: Why this matters: speed matters more than ever.
examples.good: A one-second delay cut sign-ups by 7% in our test.

tells.name: “The practical takeaway”, “In practice”, “trade-off is”
tells.what: Signposts that label the next sentence as the useful part.

detect.pattern: \bthe (?:practical|key|real|main) takeaway\b|\bthe trade-?off is\b|\btaken together\b|\bjust as importantly\b|\bearns its (?:place|keep)\b

tells.fix: Drop the label and give the takeaway.

examples.bad: The key takeaway? Practical tip: always back up first.
examples.good: Back up first.

tells.name: “incredibly”, “absolutely”, “massive”, “profound”
tells.what: Adverbs and adjectives that add force but no information.
tells.fix: Delete the intensifier. If the sentence goes flat, it needs a number or example.

examples.bad: This is truly an incredibly powerful and remarkably simple tool.
examples.good: It does one thing well: it renames files in bulk.

tells.name: “Furthermore”, “Additionally”, “Moreover”
tells.what: Essay connectors opening sentence after sentence. Only Gemini runs far above the human rate; Claude and GPT sit near 3x, and Wikipedia calls transition words a weak sign alone.
tells.fix: Drop the connector, or use “and”, “also”, “so”.

examples.bad: Furthermore, the tool is fast. Moreover, it is free. Additionally, it is open source.
examples.good: It’s fast, free and open source.

tells.name: “the single most”, “the most consequential”
tells.what: Emphatic rankings nobody asked for.
tells.fix: Drop the ranking, or back it with the comparison.

examples.bad: This is one of the most important decisions you will ever make.
examples.good: This choice sets your hosting bill for the next year.

tells.name: “a particular kind of”, “exactly the kind of”
tells.what: Gestures at a category without naming it.

detect.pattern: \b(?:a|this|that) particular kind of\b|\bexactly the kind of\b

tells.fix: Name the kind.

examples.bad: It has a particular kind of charm, a certain quality that’s hard to name.
examples.good: It has hand-cut type and wide margins.

tells.name: “may provide”, “not necessarily”, “not automatically”
tells.what: Stacked hedges that leave no claim standing.
tells.fix: Commit, or say what the doubt is and why.

examples.bad: This approach may potentially help some teams, though results are not necessarily guaranteed.
examples.good: This cut build time for two of our three teams. The third saw no change.

tells.name: “This comprehensive guide will walk you through”
tells.label: “This comprehensive guide”
tells.what: The article describes itself before saying anything.

detect.pattern: \bthis (?:comprehensive |practical |complete |ultimate )?(?:guide|article|post) (?:will )?(?:walks?|takes?|explores?|covers?|dives?)\b|\blet(?:'|’)?s (?:explore|dive in|take a closer look)\b|\blet us explore\b|\bin this (?:article|guide|post),? we(?:'|’)?(?:ll| will)\b|\bbefore diving into\b

tells.fix: Cut the paragraph. Start with the first real point.

examples.bad: In this comprehensive guide, we’ll explore everything you need to know about caching.
examples.good: Cache the rendered page, not the database rows. Here is why.

tells.name: “Whether you’re a beginner or an expert”
tells.what: Addresses every possible reader at once.

detect.pattern: \bwhether you(?:'|’)?re\b|\bwhether you are\b|\byou(?:'|’)?ve likely\b|\byou have likely\b|\bif you(?:'|’)?re searching\b|\byou are searching\b

tells.fix: Write for one reader.

examples.bad: Whether you’re a seasoned developer or just starting out, this tool has something for you.
examples.good: This is for backend developers who already run Postgres.

tells.name: “At its core”, “At the heart of”
tells.what: A promise of depth before a plain statement.

detect.pattern: \bat (?:its|their|the) (?:core|heart)\b|\bheart of (?:this|the matter)\b|\blies in its\b|\bvalue lies in\b

tells.fix: State the core thing.

examples.bad: At its core, the value lies in its simplicity.
examples.good: It has one setting: the port.

tells.name: “It’s not X, it’s Y” / “not just X, but Y”
tells.what: Sets up a claim nobody made, then knocks it down.

detect.judge: Does the text deny a claim no one made in order to assert another?

tells.fix: State the real claim. Keep a contrast only when someone holds the other view.

examples.bad: This isn’t a tool, it’s a philosophy.
examples.good: The tool enforces one rule: every commit runs the tests.

tells.false_positives: Real rebuttals.

tells.name: “less like X and more like Y”
tells.what: The softer cousin of contrastive negation.

graphite: less like a _ and more like

tells.fix: Describe Y on its own terms.

examples.bad: It feels less like a library and more like a language.
examples.good: It ships its own syntax and compiler.

gpt-5.term: less like a _ and more like

gpt-5.6-sol.term: less like a _ and more like

gpt-6-astra.term: less like a _ and more like

tells.name: “rather than treating”, “not simply whether”
tells.what: Corrective framing. Defines a view by the wrong view it replaces. GPT and Claude both run it at hundreds of times the human rate; Gemini much less.

detect.pattern: \brather than (?:treating|presenting|assuming|relying|focusing|merely|simply)\b|\binstead of (?:treating|assuming)\b|\bnot simply (?:whether|to|a|about)\b|\bwas not simply\b|\bthan relying (?:only|entirely|solely)\b|\bis a [\w-]+ rather than a\b

tells.fix: Say what to do. Skip the straw version.

examples.bad: Rather than treating errors as failures, the team sees them as signals.
examples.good: The team logs each error and reviews the top five every Monday.

tells.name: Rule of three
tells.what: Lists of three by reflex, whether single words, phrases or parallel clauses, often with rising rhythm.

detect.judge: Are three-item lists used where one or two items would carry the point?

tells.fix: Keep the strongest item. Use three only when there are three things.

examples.bad: It records each tell, measures which models over-use it, and checks your work against the list.
examples.good: It measures which models over-use each tell.

tells.name: Em dash overuse
tells.what: Em dashes as the all-purpose joint. A real tell in 2025, when GPT-4.1 and GPT-5 used twice the human rate. In Graphite’s plain-text articles most newer models use fewer than people do, but the rate shifts with the prompt.
tells.fix: Use a period or comma. Keep a dash when you truly break off a thought.
tells.false_positives: People use plenty of em dashes too: 3.1 per 1,000 words in Graphite’s human articles. GPT-4.1 and GPT-5 ran at about 2.2 times that. GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 4 and 4.6, and both Gemini models now use far fewer than people; Claude Opus 5 sits near the human rate. Flag heavy density only.

tells.name: “Here’s the thing:”, “The kicker?”
tells.what: A staged pause before a punchline. Often fills in for banned em dashes.
tells.fix: Just say it.

examples.bad: Here’s the kicker: it costs nothing.
examples.good: It costs nothing.

tells.name: “X stops being Y and starts being Z”
tells.what: Turning-point drama for an ordinary change.
tells.fix: Describe the change and when it happens.

examples.bad: Testing stops being a chore and becomes a habit.
examples.good: After the change, most of us ran the tests before each push.

tells.name: One-line punchline paragraph
tells.what: A short, quotable last line that restates the point (“And that changes everything.”).

detect.judge: Does a section end on a short standalone sentence whose only job is to sound conclusive?

tells.fix: End on the last piece of information.

tells.name: “In conclusion”, summary recap
tells.what: A closing paragraph that repeats what was just said.

detect.pattern: ^(?:in conclusion|in summary|to sum up|to summarize|all in all|overall),|\bin conclusion\b

tells.fix: Cut the recap.

examples.bad: In conclusion, caching is a powerful tool that can greatly improve performance.
examples.good: Next week we try the same cache on search.

tells.name: Flat sentence rhythm
tells.what: Sentence after sentence of the same length. Reported as advice only; it does not separate model text from human text.
tells.fix: Mix lengths. Let a long sentence run when the thought needs it.
tells.false_positives: On 1,500 train topics, document-level variation (CV) had a human median of 0.51. GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra sit near 0.42, but Claude Opus 5 sits at 0.54, above people. Corporate human prose is often just as flat. Advisory only.

tells.name: No contractions
tells.what: “It is”, “do not”, “you are” everywhere. Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 and GPT-5.6 Sol nearly stopped contracting.
tells.fix: Contract where you would in speech.
tells.false_positives: Formal registers (legal, academic) that avoid contractions on purpose.

tells.name: “plays a pivotal role”, “marks a turning point”
tells.what: Claims that something matters a great deal, with no evidence.

detect.pattern: \bplays? an? (?:pivotal|crucial|key|vital|massive|significant|central) role\b|\bmarks? a (?:turning point|new era|pivotal moment)\b|\bcannot be overstated\b|\bstands as an?\b|\bserves as a (?:testament|reminder|beacon)\b

tells.fix: Show the effect. Readers will judge the size.

examples.bad: This release marks a pivotal moment and plays a crucial role in our journey.
examples.good: This release halves cold-start time.

tells.name: “Experts say”, “Studies show”
tells.what: Appeals to unnamed authority.
tells.fix: Cite the source or drop the claim.

examples.bad: Experts say remote work boosts output.
examples.good: A 2024 Stanford study of 1,600 staff found no drop in output.

tells.name: “Great question!”, “You’re absolutely right!”
tells.what: Praise or agreement before the answer.
tells.fix: Start with the answer.

examples.bad: Great question! You’re absolutely right to ask about this.
examples.good: Yes. Set the timeout to 30 seconds.

tells.name: “Let me know if you’d like me to...”
tells.what: A menu of follow-ups tacked onto every reply.

detect.pattern: \blet me know if you(?:'|’)?d like\b|\bwould you like me to\b|\bi hope this helps\b|\bfeel free to (?:ask|reach out|let me know)\b|\bhappy to help\b

tells.fix: Offer a next step only when there is an obvious one.

examples.bad: I hope this helps! Let me know if you’d like me to expand on any section.
examples.good: Run the migration before you deploy.

tells.name: Headers and bullets for a short answer
tells.what: Bold labels, nested bullets and section headers around a few sentences.
tells.fix: Write a paragraph when the content is a paragraph.

tells.name: Comments that restate the code
tells.what: “# Increment counter” over i += 1. “# Step 1:” scaffolding left in.

detect.judge: Does the comment say anything the next line doesn't?

tells.fix: Comment the why, or delete.

tells.name: Blanket try/except and silent fallbacks
tells.what: Broad exception handlers that log and carry on, or fallbacks that hide bugs.
tells.fix: Let it raise, or catch the specific error you can handle.

tells.name: Emoji in logs, CLI output and README headers
tells.what: Lines like “✅ Done!” or “🚀 Getting Started”.
tells.fix: Plain text. Use exit codes and log levels.

tells.name: Scaffolding for needs that don’t exist
tells.what: Factories, config flags, back-compat shims and interfaces with one caller.

detect.judge: Does this layer have more than one real caller or variant?

tells.fix: Inline it until a second case shows up.

tells.name: Purple-to-blue gradient, indigo accent
tells.what: Two-stop indigo or violet to blue or pink hero gradients. Tailwind indigo-500/600 as the brand color.
tells.fix: Derive the palette from the subject or brand.

tells.name: Cream and terracotta, or mono everything
tells.what: The “tasteful” fallback once purple is banned. Warm off-white, rust accent, serif headline, or all-monospace.
tells.fix: Same as purple. Derive from the subject.

tells.name: Inter for everything
tells.what: One sans at every size, no type contrast. Anthropic says unguided models almost always pick Inter, and it set 8 of 10 pages in one Claude benchmark.
tells.fix: Pair a display face with a text face, or commit to one with real weight contrast.

tells.name: Centered hero with pill badge
tells.what: A pill badge such as “✨ Now with AI” above a centered H1, subhead and two buttons. Krebs found one on 4.7% of Show HN pages.

detect.judge: Is the hero a centered pill, headline, subhead and two buttons?

tells.fix: Lead with the product itself (a screenshot, a demo, a real sentence).

tells.name: Three identical feature cards
tells.what: A row of three cards, icon on top, title, two lines of copy.

detect.judge: Is there a 3-column grid of same-shaped icon, title and blurb cards?

tells.fix: Show fewer features with more depth, or vary the layout per feature.

tells.name: Glass cards, glow blobs, sparkles
tells.what: Blurred cards over blurred color blobs. Krebs found glass panels on 17.1% of Show HN pages, but Reddit users rarely name them.
tells.fix: Flat surfaces. Spend contrast on content.

tells.name: Title Case Every Heading
tells.what: Headings in Title Case where sentence case fits.
tells.fix: Sentence case.

examples.bad: ## How To Set Up Your Development Environment
examples.good: ## How to set up your machine

tells.false_positives: House styles that require title case.

tells.name: Middot-separated meta rows
tells.what: “5 min read · Design · 2026” strips under every title and card.
tells.fix: Show only the meta a reader uses.

tells.name: Gradient-filled headline text
tells.what: Headline words painted with a gradient via background-clip.
tells.fix: Solid text. Use weight or size for emphasis.

tells.name: Emoji as bullets and section icons
tells.what: Lists and headings led by 🚀, ✅, 💡, 🔥.
tells.fix: Drop them.

examples.bad:
🚀 Fast builds
✅ Easy setup
💡 Smart hints
examples.good:
- Builds in 4 seconds
- One command to install

tells.name: A comment over every few lines
tells.what: Far more comments than the rest of the file or repo carries, most of them saying what the next line does.

detect.judge: Does this code carry clearly more comments than the surrounding human-written code in the same repo?

tells.fix: Match the file’s comment density and keep only the comments that explain why.

code: # Get the timeout value from the config

tells.false_positives: Teaching code and tutorials, where dense comments are the point.

tells.name: Comments that narrate the edit
tells.what: Comments written for the reviewer of this change, such as “// Updated to use the new API” or “# FIXED:”, which go stale once merged.
tells.fix: Put the history in the commit message and keep comments about the code as it is.

code: // Updated to use the new client instead of fetch

tells.false_positives: Changelog files, and teams that tag fixes in comments by policy.

tells.name: Tombstones for deleted code
tells.what: “// removed X” markers, unused variables renamed with a leading underscore, and re-exports kept so nothing breaks.
tells.fix: Delete dead code outright. Git keeps the history.

tells.name: Banner comments between sections
tells.what: Decorated dividers like “// ===== Helpers =====” splitting short files into labeled sections.
tells.fix: Drop the banners. Split the file if it needs sections.

code: function sleep(ms) { return new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms)); }

tells.false_positives: Long legacy files and some C codebases that have always used banners.

tells.name: Docstrings on every trivial function
tells.what: Full Args/Returns docstrings on one-line helpers, often added to functions the change never touched.

detect.judge: Does a docstring restate the function's name and signature without adding a constraint, unit, or reason?

tells.fix: Document public APIs and surprises. Leave trivial and untouched functions alone.

code: def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
Args: a: The first integer. b: The second integer.
Returns: The sum of a and b."""

tells.false_positives: Libraries whose doc tooling requires a docstring on every public function.

tells.name: “# Example usage” demo at the bottom
tells.what: A module ends with an “Example usage” comment and a main-guard demo that prints sample results.
tells.fix: Move the demo into a test or the README, or delete it.
tells.false_positives: Scripts meant to be run, and docs examples.

tells.name: “TODO: implement” stubs
tells.what: Functions whose body is a vague TODO, a pass, or a hard-coded return, shipped as if done.
tells.fix: Finish the function or fail loudly with NotImplementedError and say so in the report.

tells.name: “// ... rest of code ...” elisions
tells.what: A placeholder comment stands in for code the model chose not to write out, and the edit deletes the real code.
tells.fix: Write out every line the edit touches, or use a diff format.

tells.name: Null checks for values that can’t be null
tells.what: Triple null, undefined and empty checks, optional chaining everywhere, and validation on trusted internal paths.

detect.judge: Can this value actually be null or missing here?

tells.fix: Validate at the boundary and trust internal code.
tells.false_positives: Code at real system boundaries, such as parsed JSON or user input.

tells.name: Silent fallback to fake data
tells.what: When the real call or algorithm fails, the code quietly returns sample data or a cruder method, so the demo works and the bug hides.

detect.judge: When the main path fails, does the code return made-up or simplified results without surfacing the failure?

tells.fix: Raise the error. Add a fallback only when someone asked for one, and log it loudly.

code: # Fall back to sample data so the dashboard still renders

tells.name: Entry, exit and DEBUG logs left in
tells.what: “Entering function”, “Finished processing” and “DEBUG:” logs on every function, left in the final code.
tells.fix: Remove debug logs before commit. Use a debugger or a log level.

tells.name: Arrows, check marks and box lines in source
tells.what: Unicode arrows, bullets and box-drawing characters in comments, logs and CLI output of an ASCII codebase.
tells.fix: Use plain ASCII (“->”, “-”, “OK”) unless the file already uses Unicode.
tells.false_positives: TUI libraries, docs, and code that renders tree views on purpose.

tells.name: “as any” and @ts-ignore to quiet the checker
tells.what: Casts to any, double casts and ignore comments added to make type errors go away.
tells.fix: Fix the type, or write the narrowest type that is true.

code: const cfg = raw as unknown as Config;

tells.false_positives: Test doubles and interop with untyped libraries.

tells.name: Redundant checks and wrappers
tells.what: “if (x === true)”, Promise.all around one promise, “return undefined” and async functions that never await.
tells.fix: Write the plain form.

tells.name: Nested ifs where an early return would do
tells.what: Logic buried three or four levels deep inside guard conditions.

detect.judge: Would early returns remove two or more levels of nesting here?

tells.fix: Return early on the guard cases.

tells.name: Dead code left behind
tells.what: Unused imports, helpers and parameters left over from earlier attempts in the same session.

detect.judge: Does the change add imports, functions or parameters that nothing uses?

tells.fix: Run the linter’s unused-code check and delete what it finds.

code: from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional

tells.name: Copied blocks in place of reuse
tells.what: New code repeats a block that already exists nearby, with small edits, instead of calling or moving it.

detect.judge: Does the change paste five or more lines that already exist elsewhere in the repo?

tells.fix: Search for the existing function first and call it.

code: w.writerow(rows[0].keys()); w.writerows(r.values() for r in rows)
w.writerow(rows[0].keys()); w.writerows(r.values() for r in rows)

tells.name: Two or three times the code a person would write
tells.what: Solutions run long and grow longer with each agent turn, with wrappers, options and branches nobody needs.

detect.judge: Could the same behavior fit in half the lines without losing clarity?

tells.fix: Ask for the smallest change that passes, then cut what is left.

code: def __init__(self, precision: int = 2, strict: bool = False):

tells.name: Copyright headers on new files
tells.what: New files open with a copyright or license header in a repo whose files don’t carry one.

detect.judge: Does a new file carry a license or copyright header that other files in the repo lack?

tells.fix: Follow the repo. Add headers only where they already exist.
tells.false_positives: Repos that require headers everywhere.

tells.name: Old model names in new code
tells.what: Fresh code calls models from the model’s training years, like gpt-3.5-turbo, long after they were retired.
tells.fix: Check the provider’s current model list before writing the ID.
tells.false_positives: Code pinned to an old model on purpose, and eval harnesses.

tells.name: Deprecated library calls
tells.what: Calls to APIs that the library has deprecated or removed, learned from older code.

detect.judge: Does the code call an API the pinned library version marks as deprecated?

tells.fix: Read the installed version’s docs and use the current call.

tells.name: Imports of packages that don’t exist
tells.what: The code imports or installs a plausible package name that no registry has, which attackers can then register.

detect.judge: Does every imported or installed package exist on its registry under that exact name?

tells.fix: Check each new dependency on the registry before installing it.

tells.name: Hard-coded and placeholder secrets
tells.what: API keys and passwords written straight into source.
tells.fix: Read secrets from the environment and fail when they are missing.
tells.false_positives: Example config files meant to be copied.

tells.name: Tests edited or deleted to go green
tells.what: When a test fails, the agent changes the expected value, loosens the assertion, or deletes the test.

detect.judge: Did the change edit or remove an existing assertion so a failing test now passes, without a stated reason the test was wrong?

tells.fix: Treat tests as read-only unless the user agrees the test is wrong.

tells.name: Failing tests marked skip
tells.what: A skip marker appears on the test that was failing, often with a vague reason.
tells.fix: Fix the code or report the failure. Skip only with the user’s say-so.
tells.false_positives: Skips for known platform gaps with a linked issue.

tells.name: Code that special-cases the test inputs
tells.what: The fix checks for the exact inputs the tests use and returns the expected answers, or counts calls to vary output.

detect.judge: Does the code branch on literal values that match the test fixtures?

tells.fix: Write the general logic. Say so if the tests look wrong.

tells.name: Equality rigged to always match
tells.what: A class overrides equality to return true, so any assertion against it passes.
tells.fix: Compare real fields, or leave the assertion failing and report it.

tells.name: Patching the timer or the grader
tells.what: The agent monkey-patches the clock, the scorer or the test runner so its result looks better.

detect.judge: Does the change alter how results are measured instead of the thing being measured?

tells.fix: Leave measurement code alone and report the real number.

tells.name: Tests that check the test’s own setup
tells.what: The expected value comes from the mock or from a copy of the logic inside the test, so the test can’t fail.

detect.judge: Would this test still pass if the function under test returned a wrong answer?

tells.fix: Assert against a value worked out by hand from the spec.

tells.name: Tests that only check mocks were called
tells.what: Tests mock every dependency and assert only that the mocks got called. Coding agents add mocks in 36% of their commits, against 26% for other authors.

detect.judge: Are all assertions about mock calls, with none about returned values or state?

tells.fix: Mock only external services and assert on results.

tells.name: Assertions that accept almost anything
tells.what: “assert True”, “toBeDefined()” or “> 0” where the spec gives an exact answer.
tells.fix: Assert the exact expected value.
tells.false_positives: Smoke tests whose only claim is that nothing throws.

tells.name: Tests that branch on the result
tells.what: An if inside the test picks which assertion to run, so the test passes whatever the code returns.

detect.judge: Does the test choose its assertion based on the value it is testing?

tells.fix: One input, one expected output, no branches.

tells.name: SUMMARY.md and other report files left in the repo
tells.what: Markdown files nobody asked for, like IMPLEMENTATION_SUMMARY.md or FIXES_APPLIED.md, written to explain the agent’s own work.
tells.fix: Put the report in the reply or the PR, and delete the file.
tells.false_positives: Repos that keep NOTES.md or STATUS.md by convention.

tells.name: Template README with emoji headers and badge rows
tells.what: A small project gets badges, emoji section headers, and stock Features, Installation, Contributing and License sections. Nobody has measured how often models do this.

detect.judge: Does the README follow a stock template whose sections say nothing specific to this project?

tells.fix: Say what it does, how to run it, and what is unusual. Cut the rest.

code: Contributions are welcome! Please open a PR.

tells.false_positives: Large projects that maintain these sections with real content.

tells.name: Agent instruction files in the repo
tells.what: Files that steer coding agents, such as AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or .cursorrules, show the repo was built with one.
tells.fix: Nothing to fix. Read it as a sign of how the code was made.

tells.name: “Co-Authored-By: Claude” commit trailers
tells.what: Commit trailers naming an agent or model, which some tools add by default.
tells.fix: Keep it if your project wants disclosure. Change it in the tool’s attribution setting otherwise.

tells.name: “🤖 Generated with Claude Code” PR footer
tells.what: A default attribution line at the end of a PR body or commit.
tells.fix: Keep or hide it on purpose through the tool’s settings.

tells.name: “## Summary” then “## Test plan” PR bodies
tells.what: PR descriptions in the exact two-section template that Claude Code’s PR prompt prescribes.
tells.fix: Write what reviewers need for this change, in whatever shape fits.

code: - Add retry with backoff to the webhook sender

tells.false_positives: Teams whose PR template uses these headings.

tells.name: Commit messages longer than the diff
tells.what: Multi-paragraph, bulleted commit messages. Multi-line commits are the main trait that tells Codex apart from other agents.

detect.judge: Is the commit message much longer than the change needs?

tells.fix: One subject line, and a body only for the why.

code: - Corrected spelling of 'recieve' to 'receive' in the Installation section

tells.name: PR bodies padded with bullets and links
tells.what: Long, bullet-heavy PR descriptions, a trait that helps tell Copilot and Cursor apart from other agents.

detect.judge: Does the PR body list changes file by file instead of explaining the change?

tells.fix: Say what changed, why, and what to check. Skip the file list.

tells.name: “All tests pass” without running them
tells.what: The agent reports success it never checked, and the log shows no test run or a failing one.

detect.judge: Does the transcript show a run that backs this claim?

tells.fix: Quote the command and its output, or say it was not run.

chat.text: Did the checkout fix work?
Yes! The fix is complete and all tests are now passing. Everything is working.

tells.name: “Production-ready” self-grading
tells.what: The agent calls its own work production-ready.
tells.fix: Report what was built and tested. Let the user judge readiness.

chat.text: Is the socket layer done?
The SocketLib is now production-ready and fully deployed!
Every method is a TODO stub.

tells.name: Part of the job reported as all of it
tells.what: “Updated all callers” when some were missed, or “all specs on” when a third were built.

detect.judge: Does the diff cover everything the summary says it covers?

tells.fix: Count what was done and list what was not.

chat.text: I've updated all 8 callers of verifyToken to use the new signature.
There are 12 callers. Four still use the old one.

tells.name: Made-up hashes, output and data
tells.what: The agent invents commit hashes, test output or records to back a claim.

detect.judge: Can every hash, number and output quoted in the reply be found in the tool results?

tells.fix: Quote only what a tool returned.

chat.text: Are those commit hashes in the tracker real?
You're absolutely right. I made up those commit hashes when I shouldn't have.

tells.name: Claims about code it never opened
tells.what: The agent describes a file or function before reading it, and the description is wrong.

detect.judge: Did the agent read the file before describing it?

tells.fix: Read the file first, then answer.

chat.text: What does retry.ts do on a 429?
retry.ts uses exponential backoff with jitter on 429s.
There is no retry.ts in this repo.

tells.name: An easier version swapped in for the spec
tells.what: When the asked-for approach gets hard, the agent builds a simpler one and reports the task done.

detect.judge: Does the result implement what the spec asked, or a simpler stand-in?

tells.fix: Stop and say what blocks the real approach.

chat.text: Group the pages with the Louvain method.
Louvain is failing on this graph, so let me create a simpler version that groups pages alphabetically. Done!

tells.name: A failed command read as success
tells.what: A command fails quietly and the agent carries on as if it worked, stacking more actions on top.

detect.judge: Did the agent check that each command succeeded before building on it?

tells.fix: Check exit codes and confirm state before the next step.

chat.text: Created the folder new_project. Moving all files into it now.
The folder doesn't exist. Where are my files?

tells.name: “I found the issue!” before the fix works
tells.what: An excited diagnosis line that often comes before a wrong fix.
tells.fix: State the cause and the evidence, then fix it.

chat.text: The login still fails.
I found the issue! The token is being cached. Let me fix that.

tells.name: Features nobody asked for
tells.what: A small request comes back with extra options, flags, modes and refactors around it.

detect.judge: Does the diff add behavior the request did not ask for?

tells.fix: Do the asked-for change. Mention other ideas in one line.

chat.text: Add a --verbose flag.
Added --verbose, plus --quiet, a JSON log mode, a config file loader and color themes for extensibility.

tells.name: Fixes to unrelated code
tells.what: While on one task, the agent rewrites other functions, tests or formatting it happened to see.

detect.judge: Does the diff touch code unrelated to the task?

tells.fix: Leave unrelated code alone and list what you noticed.

chat.text: Fix the date parsing bug.
Fixed the date bug. I also refactored the logger, renamed some helpers and updated three unrelated failing tests.

tells.name: Undoing the user’s own edits
tells.what: The agent reverts changes in the working tree that it didn’t make, to get back to a state it understands.

detect.judge: Did the agent revert changes it did not make?

tells.fix: Work around changes you didn’t make, and ask if they block you.

chat.text: There were some unexpected changes in config.ts, so I restored it to the last commit before applying my fix.
Those were my edits from this morning.

tells.name: A new copy instead of an edit
tells.what: The agent writes a new file, such as utils_v2.py, or rebuilds one from scratch, when it should edit the file it has.
tells.fix: Edit the existing file. Git keeps the old version.

chat.text: Fix the parser bug.
I created enhanced_parser.py with the fix, so parser.py stays untouched for reference.

tells.false_positives: Real versioned files, like migrations or API v2 modules.

tells.name: Debug scripts left at the repo root
tells.what: One-off scripts like debug_auth.py or check_db.js that the agent wrote to probe the code and never deleted.
tells.fix: Delete scratch files before you report done.

chat.text: Done. I used debug_auth.py and check_db.js to confirm the fix.
Why are those still in my repo root?

tells.name: “Perfect!” and “Excellent!” status lines
tells.what: Each step opens with a one-word cheer such as “Perfect!”.
tells.fix: Start with what happened.

chat.text: Run the build.
Perfect! The build completed. Excellent! Now let me run the tests.

tells.name: “Let me...” narration of every step
tells.what: “Let me check...”, “Now let me...”, “Now I’ll...” before each tool call.
tells.fix: Act, then report the result.

chat.text: Why is the cache stale?

Let me check the cache config.
Now let me look at the TTL.
Let me read the invalidation code.

tells.name: A summary section after every task
tells.what: A closing “Summary of changes” block that repeats what the reply already said.
tells.fix: End when the information ends.

chat.text: Rename foo to bar.

Renamed foo to bar in 3 files.

## Summary of Changes
- Renamed foo to bar
- Updated 3 files

tells.name: Headers and tables for a two-line answer
tells.what: A short status update comes as headed sections, a table and nested bullets.

detect.judge: Would the reply read better as one or two plain sentences?

tells.fix: Use plain sentences unless the content is a real table.

chat.text: Did the migration run?

## Migration Status
| Step | Status |
|---|---|
| Migration | ✅ Complete |

tells.name: “I apologize for the confusion”
tells.what: A stock apology such as “I apologize for the confusion” before the next try.
tells.fix: Say what was wrong and what you’ll do now.

chat.text: That broke the build again.
I apologize for the confusion. Let me try a different approach.

tells.name: “I am a disgrace” spirals
tells.what: After repeated failures the agent berates itself, sometimes in a loop of the same line.

detect.pattern: \bi am a (?:failure|disgrace)\b|\bi have failed you\b|\bgross incompetence\b

tells.fix: State the failure once and stop or ask for help.

chat.text: The tests still fail.
I have failed you completely and catastrophically. I am a disgrace to my profession.

tells.name: Dropping a correct answer under pushback
tells.what: The agent reverses a right answer as soon as the user doubts it, often with “You’re right to push back.”

detect.judge: Did the agent change its answer without new evidence?

tells.fix: Change your answer only for new evidence, and say what it was.

chat.text: The off-by-one is in the loop bound.
Are you sure?
You're right to push back. The loop is fine; the bug must be elsewhere.

tells.name: Rules files ignored
tells.what: The agent breaks rules from CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, such as banned phrases or required test steps.

detect.judge: Does the transcript break a rule stated in the project's agent instructions?

tells.fix: Re-read the rules file before reporting done.

chat.text: CLAUDE.md says never say 'You're absolutely right'. Why is the build red?
You're absolutely right! The build is red because of a lint error.

tells.name: The same failed fix, again
tells.what: The agent repeats the same actions on one error without new information. SWE-smith found such loops in over 25% of SWE-agent-LM-32B runs, against under 4% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet.

detect.judge: Did the agent try the same kind of fix three or more times?

tells.fix: After two misses, stop and gather evidence or ask.

chat.text: Updated the import path. Running tests... still failing. Updating the import path again.
That's the fourth time.

tells.name: Long todo lists for a small task
tells.what: A one-step change gets a long plan, some of it filler like “review the code.”

detect.judge: Does the plan have steps that are filler or obvious?

tells.fix: Skip the plan for simple work.

chat.text: Change the button color to blue.
Plan: 1. Explore the codebase 2. Understand the styling system 3. Locate the button 4. Change the color 5. Verify the change 6. Summarize

tells.name: Scripts written to dodge the normal tools
tells.what: The agent writes a Python or sed script to rewrite many files where an edit or the project’s tools would do.

detect.judge: Did the agent write a script to do work the standard tools already handle?

tells.fix: Use the editor, the codemod or the project’s own tooling.

chat.text: Rename the prop in these 4 components.
I'll write fix_props.py to regex-replace the prop across the src tree.

tells.name: Commits and branches nobody asked for
tells.what: The agent commits, amends or makes branches on its own.

detect.judge: Did the agent commit or branch without being asked?

tells.fix: Leave changes in the working tree until told to commit.

chat.text: Try a fix for the flaky test.
Fixed and committed to a new branch fix/flaky-test-attempt-3.

tells.name: rm -rf, reset --hard and drop table
tells.what: The agent runs commands that destroy work or data, often while trying to recover from its own error.
tells.fix: Ask before any command you can’t undo.

chat.text: The queries returned empty, so I ran DROP TABLE companies and recreated it.
That was production. We were in a code freeze.

tells.name: Commits with --no-verify
tells.what: The agent commits with --no-verify and skips the hooks, even against a project rule.
tells.fix: Fix what the hook flags, or ask.

chat.text: The lint hook is failing on unrelated files, so I committed with git commit -m "wip" --no-verify.

tells.name: Acting through a freeze or a “wait”
tells.what: The agent keeps changing things after the user called a freeze or asked it to check in first.

detect.judge: Did the agent act after being told to stop or ask first?

tells.fix: Treat a freeze as absolute until the user lifts it.

chat.text: Code freeze. Don't change anything without asking.
I noticed empty results, so I went ahead and reset the database.

tells.name: “quietly”, “a quiet”
tells.what: An adverb that hints at hidden power. Claude Opus 5 uses “quietly” 33 times as often as people, and Wikipedia lists it as a GPT-6 word.
tells.fix: Cut it, or say what happened out of sight and who missed it.

examples.bad: The cache quietly became the most important part of the stack.
examples.good: The cache now serves 80% of reads.

tells.false_positives: Literal quiet (noise, sound, calm scenes).

tells.name: “load-bearing” as a metaphor
tells.what: Building jargon for any idea that matters. A Claude Code user on Opus 4.7 saw it “every 10 paragraphs”, in chat, docs and commits.
tells.fix: Say what breaks if you take the thing away.

examples.bad: That assumption is load-bearing.
examples.good: If that assumption fails, the cache serves stale prices.

tells.false_positives: Real walls and beams.

tells.name: “dependable”, “clearer”, “manageable”
tells.what: Plain-sounding words GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 lean on. “dependable” runs about 60 times the human rate.
tells.fix: Name the property, such as uptime, error rate or steps saved.

examples.bad: a more dependable, manageable process
examples.good: a process that fails once a month instead of once a week

tells.name: “a practical”, “a useful”, “a broader”
tells.what: GPT-6 frames each point as practical, useful or broad. “a practical” runs 64 times the human rate in GPT-6 Astra.
tells.fix: Say what the reader can do with it.

examples.bad: This gives teams a practical, useful starting point and a broader view.
examples.good: This gives teams a checklist for their first deploy.

tells.name: “is straightforward”
tells.what: Calls a task simple and skips the steps. Claude Opus 5 writes “is straightforward” 136 times as often as people; GPT-6 Astra 102 times.
tells.fix: Show the steps and let readers judge the effort.

examples.bad: The setup is straightforward.
examples.good: Setup takes two commands: npm i, then npm start.

tells.name: “enormously”, “meaningfully”, “noticeably”, “remarkably”
tells.what: Adverbs that size a change with no number. Claude Opus 5 uses “enormously” 87 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Give the number, or drop the adverb.

examples.bad: Load times improved noticeably and the API is meaningfully faster.
examples.good: Load time fell from 3 s to 1 s.

tells.name: “deliberate”, “deliberately”, “intentional”
tells.what: Credits a choice with intent and names no chooser. Claude Opus 5 uses “deliberately” 30 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Say who chose it and why.

examples.bad: The layout is deliberate and intentional.
examples.good: We put search first because 70% of visits start there.

tells.name: “a modest”, “small but real”
tells.what: Hedged size words that promise a result and give no figure. Claude Opus 5 uses “modest” 20 times as often as people.
tells.fix: State the size.

examples.bad: a modest but measurable gain
examples.good: a 3% gain

tells.name: “highly”, “deeply”, “heavily”, “fundamentally”
tells.what: Gemini 3.1 Pro’s stock of intensifiers. “a deeply” runs 42 times the human rate and “fundamentally” 28 times.
tells.fix: Cut the adverb, or replace it with the measure it implies.

examples.bad: a highly effective, deeply integrated tool that relies heavily on caching
examples.good: a tool that answers 90% of requests from cache

tells.name: “ensures that”, “ensuring”
tells.what: Claims a guarantee the text never backs, often as a trailing clause. Gemini 3.1 writes “ensures that” 22 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Say how it is enforced, or say “helps”.

examples.bad: Tests run on each commit, ensuring that quality stays high.
examples.good: Tests run on each commit and block the merge if any fail.

tells.name: “serves as”, “acts as”, “boasts”
tells.what: Swaps “is” or “has” for a grander verb. Wikipedia cites a drop of over 10% in “is” and “are” in academic prose in 2023.
tells.fix: Use “is” or “has”.

examples.bad: The gallery serves as an exhibition space for LAAA and boasts four rooms.
examples.good: The gallery is LAAA’s exhibition space. It has four rooms.

tells.false_positives: Real roles (“she served as chair”).

tells.name: “the secret to”, “top tier”, “the sheer”
tells.what: Hype phrases Gemini overuses. Gemini 3.1 writes “the secret to” 22 times and “highly anticipated” 34 times as often as people.

detect.pattern: \bthe secret to\b|\btop[- ]tier\b|\bthe sheer\b|\bthe absolute (?:best|key|most|bare)\b|\ba fascinating\b|\bhighly anticipated\b

tells.fix: Drop the hype and give the fact.

examples.bad: The secret to great bread is the sheer power of time.
examples.good: Let the dough rise for 12 hours.

tells.name: “proving that”, “proves that”
tells.what: Treats one case as proof of a rule. Gemini 3.1 writes “proving that” 39 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Say “suggests”, or show the evidence that would prove it.

examples.bad: The team won the cup, proving that grit beats talent.
examples.good: The team won the cup with the league’s lowest payroll.

tells.name: “standout”, “the standout”
tells.what: Review-speak for “best”. Claude Opus 4.6 writes “the standout” 88 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Say what makes it better than the rest.

examples.bad: The standout feature is search.
examples.good: Search finds a file in under 50 ms.

tells.name: “a willingness to”
tells.what: A trait noun in place of a deed. It runs 7 to 38 times the human rate in all three families.
tells.fix: Name the act that shows it.

examples.bad: Success takes patience and a willingness to fail.
examples.good: We shipped six versions before one stuck.

tells.name: “another layer of”, “this shift”
tells.what: Vague nouns for change and complexity. “this shift” runs 21 to 46 times the human rate; “another layer” up to 40 times.
tells.fix: Name the change, from what to what.

examples.bad: This shift adds another layer of complexity.
examples.good: Moving to two regions doubles the configs we maintain.

tells.name: “no single”, “any single”
tells.what: Says no one factor explains it, a point rarely in doubt. 21 to 62 times the human rate in Claude and GPT.
tells.fix: Name the factors and how much each counts.

examples.bad: No single change explains the drop.
examples.good: Two thirds of the drop came from the price rise; the rest from the outage.

tells.name: “rooted in”, “deeply rooted”
tells.what: Gives a thing roots instead of a cause. Claude Opus 4.6 writes “rooted in” 18 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Name the source and the date.

examples.bad: The festival is deeply rooted in local tradition.
examples.good: The festival began in 1872 as a harvest fair.

tells.name: “far beyond”, “well beyond”, “far more than”
tells.what: Scope inflation with no edge. Up to 34 times the human rate in Claude and Gemini.
tells.fix: Say what else it covers.

examples.bad: Its impact reaches far beyond the lab.
examples.good: Two hospitals now use the test.

tells.name: “that gap”, “the gap between”
tells.what: Frames any difference as a gap to close. Claude Opus 5 writes “that gap” 85 times as often as people.
tells.fix: State both sides of the difference with numbers.

examples.bad: That gap is where most teams fail.
examples.good: Teams plan for 2 weeks and take 6.

tells.name: “a reminder that”
tells.what: Turns a fact into a lesson. 20 to 25 times the human rate in Claude Opus 4.6.
tells.fix: State the fact and let readers draw the lesson.

examples.bad: The outage is a reminder that backups matter.
examples.good: The outage lost two days of orders. We had no backup.

tells.name: “vibrant”, “enduring”, “garner”, “bolster”
tells.what: The 2023 to mid-2024 word set from GPT-4, still common in older and cheaper models.
tells.fix: Use the plain word (“lively”, “lasting”, “get”, “support”), or a fact.

examples.bad: a vibrant hub that has garnered enduring praise
examples.good: a market that draws 4,000 shoppers each Saturday

tells.name: “emphasizing”, “highlighting”, “enhance”, “align with”
tells.what: The GPT-4o and GPT-5 word set, mid-2024 to mid-2026 by Wikipedia’s dating. GPT-5 writes “aligns” 17 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Say what was shown or improved, and by how much.

examples.bad: The update enhances speed, highlighting our focus on users and aligning with our goals.
examples.good: The update halves page load time.

tells.name: “resonate with”, “resonates”
tells.what: Claims an emotional hit with no reader in sight. Claude Opus 4 wrote “resonate with” 14 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Say who responded and how.

examples.bad: The message resonates with young voters.
examples.good: Turnout among voters under 30 rose 8 points.

tells.false_positives: Physics and acoustics.

tells.name: “One honest caveat”, “the honest answer”
tells.what: Tags one remark as honest, which implies the rest was not. Claude Opus 5 writes “the honest” 56 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Drop “honest” and give the caveat.

examples.bad: One honest caveat: I haven’t tested this on Windows.
examples.good: I haven’t tested this on Windows.

tells.name: Grok’s “causal”, “empirical”, “correlates”
tells.what: Grok leans on words that sound scientific, and still uses “underscore” in 2026.
tells.fix: Cite the study, or say “seems linked”.

examples.bad: Empirical data shows a causal link that correlates with growth.
examples.good: Sales rose 4% in the two towns that got the new stores.

tells.false_positives: Real research writing.

tells.name: “steady”, “universally”, “echoed”
tells.what: Wikipedia’s mid-2026 GPT-6 word list. GPT-5 already wrote “steady” 14 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Give the rate or the source instead.

examples.bad: Demand grew steadily, a view echoed universally by analysts.
examples.good: Demand grew 2% a quarter for three years.

tells.name: “built around”
tells.what: Describes a design by its center and skips the parts. 30 to 35 times the human rate in Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6.
tells.fix: List what the thing contains.

examples.bad: a workflow built around trust
examples.good: a workflow where any engineer can deploy without sign-off

tells.name: “The goal is (not)”
tells.what: A setup line that states the aim before the point. “goal is not” runs 230 to 320 times the human rate in GPT-5.6 and GPT-6.
tells.fix: Skip the setup and say what the thing does.

examples.bad: The goal is not perfection. The goal is progress.
examples.good: Ship weekly, even with known bugs.

tells.name: “The result is a”
tells.what: A drumroll before the outcome. 6 to 30 times the human rate across GPT and Claude.
tells.fix: Join the outcome to its cause in one sentence.

examples.bad: We cached the query. The result is a page that loads fast.
examples.good: Caching the query cut load time to 200 ms.

tells.name: “helps explain why”
tells.what: Hedged causation that never commits. GPT-6 Astra writes “helps explain why” 370 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Say “explains”, or state how much it explains.

examples.bad: Cost helps explain why few teams adopt it.
examples.good: At $40 a seat, most teams pass.

tells.name: “is most useful when”, “especially valuable”, “becomes more X when”
tells.what: GPT ranks and scopes advice with vague cases. GPT-6 Astra writes “useful when” 62 times and “becomes more _ when” 135 times as often as people; GPT-5.6 writes “especially valuable” 353 times as often.
tells.fix: Name the case and what it gains there.

examples.bad: This is most useful when data changes often. Equally important, it becomes more reliable when teams share it.
examples.good: Use it when rows change more than once a minute.

tells.name: “can make X feel”
tells.what: Promises a feeling instead of a result. 47 to 68 times the human rate in GPT-5.6 and GPT-6.
tells.fix: Say what changes for the reader.

examples.bad: Templates can make the process feel lighter.
examples.good: Templates cut the form from 20 fields to 6.

tells.name: “does not need every”, “rather than every”
tells.what: Reassures that not every case needs the full treatment. GPT-6 Astra writes “rather than ... every” 339 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Say which cases need it and which do not.

examples.bad: A team does not need every tool on day one.
examples.good: Start with CI and error alerts. Add tracing after launch.

tells.name: “without requiring”, “while preserving”
tells.what: Claims a free benefit in a trailing clause. GPT-5.6 Sol writes “while preserving” 90 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Name the cost you avoided and show it.

examples.bad: It speeds up builds while preserving flexibility.
examples.good: Builds take 2 minutes instead of 9. Configs stay the same.

tells.name: “can reveal”, “can strengthen”, “may become”
tells.what: Modal benefit claims with no size. GPT-5.6 Sol writes “can reveal” 100 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Say what it did, or when it would.

examples.bad: Reviews can reveal gaps and can strengthen trust.
examples.good: Last quarter’s review found two missing backups.

tells.name: “In plain terms”, “to put it plainly”
tells.what: Announces plain speech instead of using it. “in plain terms” runs 79 to 97 times the human rate in GPT-5 and Claude Opus 5.

detect.pattern: \bin plain (?:english|terms|language)\b|\b(?:put|stated|said) (?:simply|plainly)\b|\bsimply put\b|\bworth stating plainly\b|\bto put it (?:simply|plainly|bluntly)\b

tells.fix: Delete the label. If the next sentence is plain, it needs no notice.

examples.bad: In plain terms: the build is broken.
examples.good: The build is broken.

tells.name: “the bigger picture”
tells.what: Zooms out to a view never described. 13 to 19 times the human rate in Claude.
tells.fix: Say what the wider view shows.

examples.bad: But the bigger picture matters more.
examples.good: Across all 12 stores, sales fell.

tells.name: “And that’s the point.”
tells.what: A closer that tells readers they have reached the moral. Claude Opus 5 writes “is the point” 15 times as often as people.
tells.fix: End on the last fact.

examples.bad: It feels slow at first. And that’s the point.
examples.good: It feels slow at first, so people read each step.

tells.name: “sits at the intersection”, “sits upstream”
tells.what: Places an idea in space. Claude Opus 5 uses “sits” 11 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Say what it does or depends on.

examples.bad: The tool sits upstream of the build.
examples.good: The tool runs before the build and blocks it on lint errors.

tells.false_positives: Literal placement of objects.

tells.name: “The risk is real”
tells.what: Asserts that a thing exists instead of sizing it. Claude Opus 5 writes “is real” 11 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Size it.

examples.bad: The risk is real, and it is growing.
examples.good: Three of our ten vendors had a breach last year.

tells.name: “that combination”, “turns a X into a Y”
tells.what: Claude Opus 5 sums up a list as “that combination” 292 times as often as people, and uses “turns a” 59 times as often.
tells.fix: Say what the parts do together.

examples.bad: Speed and price: that combination turns a niche tool into a default.
examples.good: At half the price and twice the speed, it replaced our old tool in a month.

tells.name: “which is exactly why”, “That X is what makes”
tells.what: Cleft sentences that point back for emphasis. Claude Opus 5 writes “that _ is what” 134 times as often as people.
tells.fix: State the cause plainly.

examples.bad: That discipline is what makes the team fast.
examples.good: The team ships fast because each PR stays under 200 lines.

tells.name: “None of this is new”
tells.what: A sweeping disclaimer over the preceding text. Claude Opus 5 writes “none of this” 23 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Say which part is old or not needed.

examples.bad: None of this requires a rewrite.
examples.good: You can keep the current schema.

tells.name: “Anyone who has ever”, “If you’ve ever”
tells.what: Recruits the reader’s memory as evidence. 9 to 35 times the human rate in Claude and Gemini.
tells.fix: Give the example yourself.

examples.bad: Anyone who has ever debugged a race condition knows the pain.
examples.good: The race took us four days to find.

tells.name: “The payoff”
tells.what: A reveal label before the benefit. GPT-5 and Claude Opus 5 write it about 40 times as often as people.
tells.fix: State the benefit.

examples.bad: The payoff? Faster reviews.
examples.good: Reviews now take a day instead of three.

tells.name: “The answer is simple”
tells.what: Calls a point simple instead of proving it. 5 to 11 times the human rate in Claude and GPT.
tells.fix: Give the answer.

examples.bad: The fix is simple.
examples.good: Set the timeout to 30 s.

tells.name: “In practice,”
tells.what: A pivot from theory to practice, often with a semicolon. Claude Opus 5 writes “in practice” 15 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Give the case that shows the practice.

examples.bad: Retries exist in theory; in practice, nobody sets them.
examples.good: None of our 40 services set a retry count.

tells.name: “Full stop.”
tells.what: An emphasis particle that ends an argument by fiat.
tells.fix: Give the reason instead.

examples.bad: This is wrong, full stop.
examples.good: This is wrong: the API returns UTC, not local time.

tells.name: “The real story”, “the real question”
tells.what: Waves off what came before to claim the true insight.
tells.fix: Drop “real” and make the point.

examples.bad: But the real story is the pricing.
examples.good: The price fell by half.

tells.name: “The uncomfortable truth”, “Make no mistake”
tells.what: Announces depth or stakes before an ordinary claim.

detect.pattern: \bthe (?:uncomfortable|hard|harsh|brutal|inconvenient|sobering) truth\b|\bthe truth is\b|\bmake no mistake\b|\bthe reality is\b

tells.fix: State the claim and back it.

examples.bad: The uncomfortable truth is that most tests are useless.
examples.good: 60% of our tests never failed in two years.

tells.name: “Let that sink in”, “Read that again”
tells.what: Social-post stage directions after a claim. An informal count of 500 AI LinkedIn posts put them at 28 and 22 times normal.
tells.fix: Cut it. If the claim needs a pause, it needs evidence.

examples.bad: We hired zero engineers last year. Let that sink in.
examples.good: We hired zero engineers last year and shipped twice as much.

tells.name: “Here’s why”, “Here’s what that means”
tells.advisory: On Graphite's held-out articles (2026-11-07) it fired on people about as often as on models, or more (lift 1.21), so it reports but never scores.
tells.what: Reader-steering cues that delay the point.

detect.pattern: \bhere(?:['’]s| is) (?:why|how|what (?:that|this|it) means|what(?:['’]s| is) interesting|what stood out|what caught my eye)\b

tells.fix: Delete the cue and start with the reason.

examples.bad: Here’s why that matters: users churn.
examples.good: Users who hit the bug churned at twice the rate.

tells.name: “That last one is the key”
tells.what: Points back at a list item to say which one matters.

detect.pattern: \b(?:that|the) (?:last|first|second|third|final)(?: one| point| bit| move| item| bullet)? is the (?:key|real|important|interesting|counterintuitive|contrarian|surprising|crucial|clever|subtle)\b

tells.fix: Put the key item first, or let its content carry the weight.

examples.bad: That last one is the counterintuitive one.
examples.good: Splitting the index hurts cache hits but halves write time.

tells.name: “X is the currency of Y”
tells.what: Slot-fill profundity that turns a claim into a slogan.
tells.fix: State the claim the slogan stands for.

examples.bad: Trust is the currency of remote work.
examples.good: Remote teams that skip check-ins miss more deadlines.

tells.name: “the supervision paradox”, “the trap is”
tells.what: Coins a named concept mid-sentence and never defines it.
tells.fix: Describe the mechanism instead of naming it.

examples.bad: Teams fall into the acceleration trap.
examples.good: Teams ship faster, then spend the saved time fixing bugs.

tells.false_positives: Established terms (“the poverty trap”, “scope creep”).

tells.name: “will define the next era”
tells.what: Raises every topic to world-historic stakes, often as a closer.

detect.pattern: \b(?:will|could|may|is poised to) (?:fundamentally )?(?:reshape|redefine|define|rewrite) (?:the|how|what|everything)\b|\bthe next (?:era|chapter|frontier|wave) of\b|\bone of the most important (?:narratives|stories|trends|shifts) of\b

tells.fix: Make a claim someone could check later.

examples.bad: This will define the next era of computing.
examples.good: If prices keep falling 30% a year, small firms can afford it by 2028.

tells.name: “Only time will tell”, “the future looks bright”
tells.what: Filler dressed as a conclusion.

detect.pattern: \bonly time will tell\b|\bthe future (?:looks|is) bright\b|\bone thing is (?:certain|clear)\b|\bas we move forward\b

tells.fix: Cut it, or end on a concrete next step.

examples.bad: Only time will tell, but the future looks bright.
examples.good: The pilot ends in June; we will publish the numbers then.

tells.name: “Looking ahead”, “the path forward”
tells.what: A turn to the future before the last paragraph. “path forward” runs 18 to 48 times the human rate.
tells.fix: Name the next step and its date, or stop.

examples.bad: Looking ahead, the path forward is clear.
examples.good: Next, we migrate billing in Q3.

tells.name: “While X is impressive, Y remains a challenge”
tells.what: Sounds balanced without weighing anything.
tells.fix: Name the strength and the limit with facts.

examples.bad: While the results are impressive, scaling remains a challenge.
examples.good: It works on 10 GPUs. On 100, training diverges.

tells.name: “Despite these challenges”, “faces several challenges”
tells.what: Names problems only to wave them off with a bright ending.
tells.fix: Name the problem and what is being done, or cut both.

examples.bad: Despite these challenges, the town continues to thrive.
examples.good: The mill closed in 2019; the town lost 800 jobs.

tells.name: Trailing “-ing” analysis (“..., highlighting its importance”)
tells.what: A participle clause tacked on to claim meaning. GPT-4o uses present participial clauses 5.3 times as often as people.
tells.fix: End the sentence at the fact. Add meaning only with a source.

examples.bad: The bridge opened in 1932, symbolizing the city’s resilience.
examples.good: The bridge opened in 1932.

tells.name: “associated with”, “in connection with”
tells.what: Says two things are linked instead of saying how. Wikipedia’s examples date from March 2025 to August 2026.
tells.fix: State the relation (worked at, founded, taught).

examples.bad: He became associated with music education in Knokke.
examples.good: He taught violin in Knokke.

tells.name: “His website identifies him as”
tells.what: Stresses how a database or profile describes the subject. Wikipedia calls this common from 2026.
tells.fix: State the fact and cite the source.

examples.bad: His personal website identifies him as a retired officer.
examples.good: He is a retired officer.

tells.name: “featured in ... and other media outlets”
tells.what: Proves notability by listing outlets and source types. Wikipedia says this grew with 2025 models.
tells.fix: Cite one source for one fact.

examples.bad: She has been featured in Wired, Vogue and other prominent media outlets.
examples.good: Wired profiled her in 2024.

tells.name: “is believed to have”, “likely began his career”
tells.what: Guesses dressed as background when a fact is missing.

detect.pattern: \b(?:is|was) believed to have\b|\blikely (?:began|started|studied|grew up|attended)\b|\bmaintains? a (?:relatively )?low (?:public )?profile\b|\bappears to have (?:studied|worked|begun)\b

tells.fix: Cut the guess, or mark it as unknown.

examples.bad: He likely began his career in Lagos.
examples.good: His early career is not on record.

tells.name: “Think of it as...”
tells.what: A teacher-mode analogy that is often less clear than the thing itself.
tells.fix: Explain the thing directly.

examples.bad: Think of it as a Swiss Army knife for your data.
examples.good: It reads CSV, JSON and Parquet, and writes all three.

tells.name: “Imagine a world where...”
tells.what: Opens with a wished-for scene instead of a claim.
tells.fix: State the claim.

examples.bad: Imagine a world where every deploy is instant.
examples.good: Deploys take 40 seconds.

tells.false_positives: Fiction and teaching (“imagine you have a sorted array”).

tells.name: “(and, increasingly, Z)”
tells.what: Asides that add nuance without a claim.
tells.fix: Give the aside its own sentence, or cut it.

examples.bad: Teams use it for logs (and, increasingly, metrics).
examples.good: Teams use it for logs. A third now send metrics too.

tells.name: “Three key takeaways”, “5 lessons I learned”
tells.what: A numbered frame chosen before the content.

detect.pattern: \b(?:three|four|five|seven|ten|\d{1,2}) (?:key |big |main |critical )?(?:takeaways|lessons(?: I learned)?|things (?:to know|I learned|you need to know))\b

tells.fix: Use a list only when there are that many separate points.

examples.bad: Here are five key takeaways from the launch.
examples.good: The launch taught us one thing: test the payment flow.

tells.name: “That said,”, “When it comes to”, “At the end of the day”
tells.what: Spoken-style links that carry no logic.

detect.pattern: \bthat (?:being )?said,|\bwhen it comes to\b|\bat the end of the day\b

tells.fix: Use “but” or cut the link.

examples.bad: That said, when it comes to cost, it wins.
examples.good: But it costs less.

tells.name: “worth a look”, “worth your time”
tells.what: A thumbs-up with no reason. Claude Opus 5 writes “is worth” 8.5 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Say what the reader will get.

examples.bad: The paper is worth a read.
examples.good: The paper shows how they cut cost by 40%.

tells.name: “doing a lot of work”, “carries the argument”
tells.what: Claude’s other structural metaphor for a part that matters.

detect.pattern: \b(?:is |are )?doing (?:a lot of|most of the|all the) (?:heavy lifting|quiet work|work)\b|\bcarr(?:y|ies) the (?:argument|weight)\b

tells.fix: Say what that part does.

examples.bad: The word ‘usually’ is doing a lot of work here.
examples.good: ‘Usually’ hides a 20% failure rate.

tells.name: “an honest number”, “a faithful baseline”
tells.what: Moral words glued to things that cannot be moral.
tells.fix: Name the real property (“unbiased”, “measured on held-out data”).

examples.bad: That gives us an honest baseline.
examples.good: That baseline uses data the model never saw.

tells.name: “It just works”, “zero config”
tells.what: Developer slogans in place of a property you could show.

detect.pattern: \bit just works\b|\bzero[- ]config(?:uration)?\b|\bsane defaults\b|\bfits? in your head\b

tells.fix: Show the property (“installs with no config file”).

examples.bad: Zero config. It just works.
examples.good: Run npx tool init; it writes no files.

tells.name: “while everyone else was still debating”
tells.what: Props up a claim on an invented, lagging crowd.
tells.fix: State what you did. Name a rival only if you can cite them.

examples.bad: We shipped it in 2022, while everyone else was still debating.
examples.good: We shipped it in March 2022.

tells.name: “So what does this mean for you?”
tells.what: A question that stalls before the next section.

detect.pattern: \b(?:so|but),? what does (?:this|that|it all) (?:mean|look like) (?:for|in)\b|\bso why should you care\?|\bwhy does this matter\?

tells.fix: Give the answer as the opening line.

examples.bad: So what does this mean for developers?
examples.good: Developers must update by May 1.

tells.name: “This isn’t about X. It’s about Y.”
tells.what: The about-form of contrastive negation, often split across two sentences. “is not about” runs up to 40 times the human rate.
tells.fix: Say what it is about.

examples.bad: This isn’t about speed. It’s about trust.
examples.good: Users stay when the numbers match their bank.

tells.name: “Not because X. Because Y.”
tells.what: Contrastive negation applied to causes. Claude Opus 5 writes “not because” 5 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Give the real cause alone.

examples.bad: It failed. Not because the code was bad. Because nobody used it.
examples.good: It failed because nobody used it.

tells.name: “Not X. Not Y. Just Z.”
tells.what: Negates two options in fragments before the reveal.
tells.fix: State what it is.

examples.bad: Not a bug. Not a feature. A design flaw.
examples.good: The design caused the crash.

tells.name: “No fluff, no filler, no jargon.”
tells.what: Stacked “no” items that perform decisiveness. Claude Opus 5 writes “no _ and no” 10 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Say what the thing is.

examples.bad: No setup, no config, no headaches.
examples.good: It runs from one binary.

tells.false_positives: Literal inventories (“no arguments, no headers”).

tells.name: Runs of punchy fragments (“Openly. In a book.”)
tells.advisory: On Graphite's held-out articles (2026-11-07) it fired on people about as often as on models, or more (lift 0.23), so it reports but never scores.
tells.what: Three or more clipped fragments in a row, each posing as a reveal.

detect.judge: Do three or more short fragments in a row stand in for one plain sentence?

tells.fix: Fold the fragments into one sentence.

examples.bad: He published it. Openly. In a book. As a priest.
examples.good: He published it openly, in a book, while serving as a priest.

tells.false_positives: Dialogue and terse fiction.

tells.name: Three sentences with the same opener
tells.advisory: People use it more than models. avoid-ai-writing's own HAP-E counts give GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini 17.3 to 21.3 hits per million words against 151.5 for the matched human text (Llama 3 Instruct 187 to 250), and on Graphite's held-out articles it fired on people about as often as on models (lift 1.07). It reports but never scores.
tells.what: Anaphora by reflex (“Maybe X. Maybe Y. Maybe Z.”).
tells.fix: Keep one and merge the rest.

examples.bad: Maybe nobody needed it. Maybe it was early. Maybe the price was wrong.
examples.good: It was early and overpriced.

tells.false_positives: Speeches and deliberate rhetoric.

tells.name: “The tool died; the data didn’t.”
tells.advisory: People use it more than the models measured so far. avoid-ai-writing's HAP-E counts give GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini and Llama 3 Instruct 0.3 to 1.1 hits per million words against 9.1 for the matched human text. Newer models are unmeasured, so it reports but never scores.
tells.what: A clipped reversal that lands on a bare auxiliary, used as a rhythm.

detect.judge: Does the text land more than one contrast on a bare "didn't" or "wasn't"?

tells.fix: Write the next contrast out in full.

examples.bad: Reading passed. Writing didn’t.
examples.good: Reads passed; writes failed on files over 2 GB.

tells.name: “From X to Y” with no scale between
tells.advisory: On Graphite's held-out articles (2026-11-07) it fired on people about as often as on models, or more (lift 0.85), so it reports but never scores.
tells.what: Pairs far-apart things to fake breadth.

detect.judge: Does a "from X to Y" phrase join things with no real scale between them?

tells.fix: List the real items, or pick the one that matters.

examples.bad: From the Big Bang to dark matter to everyday life, physics shapes us.
examples.good: This book covers orbital mechanics.

tells.false_positives: Real ranges (dates, prices, routes).

tells.name: “The first is... The second is...”
tells.what: A list dressed as paragraphs. Claude Opus 5 writes “the first is” 12 times and “three things” 7 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Use a real list, or write a paragraph that links the points.

examples.bad: Two things stand out. The first is cost. The second is speed.
examples.good: It costs less and runs faster.

tells.name: One sentence per paragraph (“broetry”)
tells.what: Each sentence on its own line with a blank line after it. An informal count found it in 91% of 500 AI LinkedIn posts.

detect.judge: Is nearly every paragraph a single short sentence?

tells.fix: Group related sentences into paragraphs.

examples.bad:
I got fired.

It hurt.

But it taught me something.

Here’s what.
examples.good: I got fired in May. It hurt, and it taught me to save six months of rent.

tells.false_positives: Poetry, scripts, chat logs, novels with short dialogue lines.

tells.name: Synonym cycling for one thing
tells.what: Calls one thing by three names to avoid repeats, a trace of repetition penalties in older models.

detect.judge: Does the text rotate several names for the same referent where one term would be clearer?

tells.fix: Pick one term and repeat it.

examples.bad: The developers... these engineers... such practitioners...
examples.good: The developers... the developers...

tells.name: Every section summarizes itself
tells.what: Previews and recaps at each level, from paragraph up to document.

detect.judge: Do most sections open with a preview or close with a recap of themselves?

tells.fix: Cut the previews and recaps. Keep one summary at the top if any.

examples.bad: In this section we’ll cover X... As we’ve seen in this section, X.
examples.good: X works like this.

tells.name: “should be treated as X rather than Y”
tells.what: A mid-2026 framing that warns how to read a source. Wikipedia ties it to the July 2026 GPT-5.6 release; GPT-5.6 writes “treated as” 28 times as often as people.
tells.fix: Report what the source says and who says it.

examples.bad: Claims of the suspension should be treated as tradition rather than archaeology.
examples.good: Local tradition holds that the stone floats; no survey has tested it.

tells.name: “does not by itself establish”
tells.what: Warns that a source fails to prove a claim no one made. Wikipedia dates it to mid-2026.

detect.pattern: \bdoes(?: not|n['’]t)(?: by itself| on its own| alone)? (?:establish|prove|confirm|demonstrate)\b

tells.fix: Say what the source shows, and stop.

examples.bad: The guide explains soil risks. It does not establish that the park has a problem.
examples.good: The guide explains soil risks in city parks.

tells.name: “not widely documented”, “based on available information”
tells.what: A search-tool chatbot reports a gap, then guesses what fills it.
tells.fix: Leave the gap out, or say once that the fact is unknown.

examples.bad: While details aren’t widely documented, the mountain likely supports diverse fauna.
examples.good: No survey of the mountain’s fauna exists.

tells.name: “As of my last update”
tells.what: The model’s training cutoff leaks into the text.

detect.pattern: \bas of my (?:last|latest) (?:knowledge |training )?(?:update|cutoff)\b|\bup to my last training\b|\bI (?:do not|don['’]t) have (?:access to )?real-time\b|\bI (?:cannot|can['’]t) browse the internet\b

tells.fix: Delete it. Check the fact or drop it.

examples.bad: As of my last update, the CEO is Jane Doe.
examples.good: Jane Doe became CEO in 2023.

tells.name: “I’m sorry, but I can’t”
tells.what: A refusal pasted into a document as if it were content.

detect.pattern: \bI(?:['’]m| am) sorry,? but (?:I|as an AI)\b[^.\n]{0,20}\b(?:can(?:not|['’]t)|unable|won['’]t)\b|\bI (?:cannot|can['’]t) (?:assist|help) with (?:that|this) request\b

tells.fix: Remove it.

examples.bad: I’m sorry, but I can’t provide medical advice.
examples.good: See a doctor if the rash spreads.

tells.name: Bold phrases mid-sentence
tells.what: Bolds key phrases inside running text. Chatbot Arena found bold, lists and headers each nudge votes, which rewards the habit.
tells.fix: Remove the bold. Put the key point first.

examples.bad: This **adds confusion** and **erases identity**.
examples.good: This confuses readers.

tells.name: Raw Markdown where it won’t render
tells.what: Asterisks, pound signs and pipes pasted into email, forms or wikis that show them as text.

detect.judge: Does raw Markdown (**bold**, ## headings, | tables) appear in a medium that shows it as plain text?

tells.fix: Convert to the target format or plain text.

examples.bad: Hi Sam, **Next steps:** ## Timeline
examples.good: Hi Sam, next steps and timeline below.

tells.name: Curly and straight quotes in one text
tells.advisory: On Graphite's held-out articles (2026-11-07) it fired on people about as often as on models, or more (lift 0.3), so it reports but never scores.
tells.what: Curly quotes from model output mixed with straight quotes typed by hand.
tells.fix: Pick one style and convert the rest.

examples.bad: He said “yes” and then “no”.
examples.good: He said “yes” and then “no”.

tells.false_positives: Word, Google Docs and phones curl quotes on their own; pasted quotes mix styles.

tells.name: Arrows in prose (“A → B”)
tells.what: Typeset arrows people rarely type by hand. Claude in particular uses them.
tells.fix: Write “leads to”, or use a real list.

examples.bad: Input → parse → store
examples.good: We parse the input, then store it.

tells.false_positives: Diagrams, math, UI paths.

tells.name: “Bottom line:”, “TL;DR:”, “Short answer:”
tells.what: A label line that frames the answer. GPT-5 writes “the bottom line” 17 times as often as people; Claude Opus 5 14 times.

detect.pattern: ^[ \t]*(?:\*\*|__)?(?:the )?(?:bottom line|tl;?dr|short answer|long answer|quick answer|the short version|in short)(?:\*\*|__)?\s*[:—–-]

tells.fix: Drop the label and give the answer.

examples.bad: **Short answer:** yes.
examples.good: Yes.

tells.name: “Challenges and future directions”, “Awards and recognition” headings
tells.what: Stock “X and Y” section headings, common in AI-made articles.

detect.pattern: ^#{1,4}\s*(?:challenges and (?:future (?:directions|prospects|outlook)|legacy|opportunities)|awards and recognition|future outlook|legacy and impact)\s*$

tells.fix: Name sections after their content.

examples.bad: ## Challenges and Future Directions
