examples.good: ## Funding ends in 2027

tells.name: A block of six or more hashtags
tells.what: Broad tags trailed after a short post.
tells.fix: Keep two or three specific tags, or none.

examples.bad: #AI #Tech #Innovation #Future #Growth #Leadership
examples.good: #rustlang

tells.name: Chatbot citation tokens (“oaicite”, “turn0search0”, “[cite: 3]”)
tells.what: Internal citation markup from ChatGPT, Gemini or DeepSeek, pasted unedited.
tells.fix: Strip the tokens and add real citations.

examples.bad: Sales rose 4% [cite: 3, 12].
examples.good: Sales rose 4% (Q3 report, p. 2).

tells.name: “utm_source=chatgpt.com” in links
tells.what: Tracking tags that AI tools add to links they cite.
tells.fix: Strip the tracking parameter.

examples.bad: https://example.com/report?utm_source=chatgpt.com
examples.good: https://example.com/report

tells.name: “[Your Name]”, “[Insert source]”
tells.what: Template slots the user forgot to fill.
tells.fix: Fill the slot or cut the sentence.

examples.bad: Best regards, [Your Name]
examples.good: Best regards, Priya

tells.false_positives: Real templates.

tells.name: “Here’s a polished version”, “Here’s the clean version”
tells.what: The chatbot’s hand-off line, pasted along with the text.
tells.fix: Delete the hand-off line.

examples.bad: Here’s a polished version of your bio: Jane is a designer...
examples.good: Jane is a designer...

tells.name: “Improved clarity and flow”
tells.what: Edit, commit or PR summaries that claim style gains and rule compliance.
tells.fix: Say what changed (“split the intro; fixed two dates”).

examples.bad: Refined wording, improved clarity and flow, ensured adherence to guidelines.
examples.good: Fixed the birth year and cut two promo lines.

tells.name: “If you want, I can...”, “Want me to...?”
tells.what: GPT-5-era teaser offers at the end of each reply. In March 2026 OpenAI said a GPT-5.3 Instant update “reduces teaser-style phrasing”.

detect.pattern: \bif you(?:['’]d)? (?:want|like),? I(?:['’]ll| can| could| will)\b|(?:^|[.!?]\s+)want me to\b|\byou(?:['’]ll| will) never believe\b

tells.fix: End when the answer ends.

examples.bad: If you want, I can also turn this into a checklist.
examples.good: (End of reply.)

tells.name: “I’ll do X next unless you say otherwise”
tells.what: An agent names its own next task and makes the user opt out.

detect.pattern: \bnext unless you (?:say|tell me) otherwise\b|\bunless you(?:['’]d)? (?:prefer|rather|object),? I(?:['’]ll| will)\b

tells.fix: Report the open item as a fact and stop.

examples.bad: I’ll re-review PR 12 next unless you say otherwise.
examples.good: PR 12 still has no review.

tells.name: “I’ll be honest”, “Honestly?”, “Look,”
tells.advisory: On Graphite's held-out articles (2026-11-07) it fired on people about as often as on models, or more (lift 0.35), so it reports but never scores.
tells.what: Sincerity announced instead of shown. Users filed Claude Code issues against “I want to be honest” in 2026.

detect.pattern: \bI(?:['’]ll| will| want to) be (?:honest|direct|blunt|upfront|straight)(?: with you)?\b|\blet['’]s be (?:honest|real)\b|\bto be (?:fully |completely )?(?:honest|transparent|frank)\b|(?:^|[.!?]\s+)(?:and )?(?:honestly|frankly)\?|(?:^|[.!?]\s+)(?:look|real talk),

tells.fix: Delete the announcement and say the thing.

examples.bad: I’ll be honest with you: the plan won’t work.
examples.good: The plan won’t work: it needs twice the budget.

tells.false_positives: Mid-sentence “honestly” in casual speech.

tells.name: “Two caveats I’d rather flag than let you discover”
tells.what: A clause that advertises a coming disclosure.

detect.judge: Does a clause announce that the writer is being forthcoming, separate from the disclosure itself?

tells.fix: Cut the frame and keep the disclosure.

examples.bad: Two caveats I’d rather flag now than let you discover later: ...
examples.good: Two caveats: ...

tells.name: “A few things stand out”, “What struck me”
tells.what: A stock reaction frame before the list.

detect.pattern: \b(?:a few|two|three|several) things stand out\b|\bwhat stands out (?:most )?(?:is|here)\b|\bwhat struck me (?:most )?(?:was|is)\b|\bwhat surprised me most\b

tells.fix: Start with the first point.

examples.bad: A few things stand out. First, the tests are flaky.
examples.good: The tests are flaky.

tells.name: “Let’s break this down”, “Let’s unpack this”
tells.what: A teacher-voice opener that delays the point.
tells.fix: Start with the first step.

examples.bad: Let’s break this down step by step.
examples.good: First, the request hits the load balancer.

tells.name: “You’re asking about...”, “To answer your question”
tells.what: Restates the prompt before answering.

detect.pattern: ^[ \t]*(?:you(?:['’]re| are) asking (?:about|whether|how)|to answer your question|so,? you(?:['’]re| are) (?:asking|wondering))\b
detect.judge: Does the reply restate the question before any new information?

tells.fix: Start with the answer.

examples.bad: You’re asking about retries. Retries are how the client handles failure.
examples.good: The client retries five times.

tells.name: “Let me think step by step”
tells.what: Chain-of-thought scaffolding left in a final answer.

detect.pattern: \blet me think (?:this through|step by step|about this)\b|\bhere(?:['’]s| is) my thought process\b|\bto approach this systematically\b|\bworking through this logically\b

tells.fix: Keep the conclusion and the evidence. Cut the narration.

examples.bad: Let me think step by step. First, consider the input...
examples.good: The input is unsorted, so binary search fails.

tells.name: “Now I have the complete picture”
tells.what: An agent reports on its own state between tool calls.
tells.fix: Report the findings and drop the status line.

examples.bad: Now I have the complete picture. The bug is in auth.
examples.good: The bug is in auth.ts line 40.

tells.name: “Sit with that”, “That’s not nothing”
tells.what: Essayist tics that announce depth instead of giving it.

detect.pattern: \bsit with (?:that|this|it)(?: for a moment)?\b|\bthat(?:['’]s| is) not nothing\b|\byou already know (?:the answer|this)\b|\bdon['’]t take my word for it\b|(?:^|[.!?]\s+)turns out,?

tells.fix: State the claim and its size.

examples.bad: You cut costs by 10%. That’s not nothing.
examples.good: You cut costs by 10%, about $40k a year.

tells.name: “You’re picking up on something few people notice”
tells.what: Tells the user their question shows rare insight. Successor to “Great question!”.

detect.pattern: \b(?:very )?few people (?:ever )?(?:notice|see|ask|realize|catch)\b|\bthat(?:['’]s| is) (?:rare|a rare (?:insight|level of))\b|\byou(?:['’]re| are) (?:cutting|getting) (?:right )?to the (?:core|heart)\b|\bnow you(?:['’]re| are) thinking like\b|\byou(?:['’]re| are) not broken\b

tells.fix: Answer the question.

examples.bad: You’re picking up on a pattern very few people notice.
examples.good: Yes, the two graphs share an axis error.

tells.name: “You’re right to call me out”, “I own that”
tells.what: Ritual contrition before the fix.

detect.pattern: \byou(?:['’]re| are) right to (?:call (?:me|that) out|push back|flag (?:this|that))\b|\bI own that\b|\bthat(?:['’]s| is) on me\b

tells.fix: Fix the error and say what changed.

examples.bad: You’re right to call me out on that. I own that.
examples.good: Corrected: the limit is 100, not 1,000.

tells.name: “Most people think X. They’re wrong.”
tells.what: The top LinkedIn opener in an informal count of 500 AI posts (38%).
tells.fix: State your claim and your evidence.

examples.bad: Most people think cold email is dead. They’re wrong.
examples.good: Our cold emails got a 9% reply rate last quarter.

tells.name: “What nobody tells you about X”
tells.what: Claims secret knowledge where none exists.

detect.pattern: \b(?:what|the (?:part|thing)) (?:nobody|no one) (?:tells you|talks about|mentions)\b|\bnobody(?:['’]s| is) (?:talking about|naming)\b|\bhere(?:['’]s| is) what (?:nobody|no one|most people)\b

tells.fix: Give the fact and drop the scarcity claim.

examples.bad: Here’s what nobody tells you about hiring.
examples.good: Half our hires came from referrals.

tells.name: “This one is worth your time:”
tells.what: A generic sign-off that vouches for a link with no reason.

detect.pattern: \bthis one(?:['’]s| is) (?:worth your time|a must-read)\b|\bdo yourself a favou?r and\b|\b(?:save|bookmark) this (?:for later|post)\b|\bthank me later\b|\bdon['’]t sleep on this\b

tells.fix: Say what the link shows, or post it bare.

examples.bad: This one is worth your time:
examples.good: How Figma cut build times by 60%:

tells.name: “The line I keep coming back to”
tells.what: Claims a quote has held the writer’s mind before showing why.

detect.pattern: \bI keep coming back to\b|\bI can['’]t stop thinking about\b|\bstill thinking about this\b|\brattling around (?:in )?my head\b

tells.fix: Quote the line and say what it explains.

examples.bad: The line I keep coming back to: agents are teenagers.
examples.good: Agents act like teenagers: they ignore rules they weren’t shown.

tells.what: Introduces a product like a game-show contestant.

examples.good: Flowdesk is a treasury dashboard.

tells.name: “*chef’s kiss*”, “(yes, really)”, “hot take:”
tells.what: Props from a canned casual voice: stage directions, winks and label openers.

detect.pattern: \*(?:chef['’]s kiss|checks notes|mic drop|sips (?:coffee|tea))\*|\((?:yes|no),? (?:really|seriously)\)|(?:^|[.!?]\s+)(?:hot take|unpopular opinion|plot twist)\s*:|\bbecause of course it does\b|\bhits different\b|\bchef['’]s kiss\b

tells.fix: Cut the prop and keep the observation.

examples.bad: The new API? *chef’s kiss*
examples.good: The new API needs one call where the old one needed four.

tells.name: Stock names and settings: Elara, Kael, Elias the lighthouse keeper
tells.what: The names, jobs and places models reach for. Elias, Mara, Elara, lighthouse and clockmaker are among 11 words found in 88% of 20,000 sampled stories.
tells.fix: Pick names that fit the setting, era and family.

examples.good: Dot Halloran stepped into the bait shop.

tells.false_positives: Real people and established characters (Pullman’s Lyra).

tells.what: The second most common slop phrase in the antislop corpus (19,295 hits).

detect.pattern: \b(?:voice|words?) (?:barely|scarcely|little more than|hardly) (?:above |more than )?a whisper\b|\bvoice barely audible\b

tells.fix: Show who strains to hear, or cut the tag.

examples.bad: “Stay,” she said, her voice barely above a whisper.

models.rules:
## Writing tells to avoid (tuned for GPT-4.1)

Readers spot these patterns as machine-made. Write the plain version instead.

- "This comprehensive guide will walk you through" → Cut the paragraph. Start with the first real point. Instead of "In this comprehensive guide, we'll explore everything you need to know about caching", write "Cache the rendered page, not the database rows. Here is why".
- "It's not X, it's Y" / "not just X, but Y" → State the real claim. Keep a contrast only when someone holds the other view. Instead of "This isn't a tool, it's a philosophy", write "The tool enforces one rule: every commit runs the tests".
- "less like X and more like Y" → Describe Y on its own terms. Instead of "It feels less like a library and more like a language", write "It ships its own syntax and compiler".
- "That distinction matters", "Why X matters" → Show what goes wrong without it. Readers will see that it matters. Instead of "Why this matters: speed matters more than ever", write "A one-second delay cut sign-ups by 7% in our test".
- "is straightforward" → Show the steps and let readers judge the effort. Instead of "The setup is straightforward", write "Setup takes two commands: npm i, then npm start".
- "genuinely", "a genuine", "is a genuinely" → Delete it. If the claim needs it to be believed, add evidence instead. Instead of "This is a genuinely useful tool", write "This tool saved us a day per release".
- "plays a pivotal role", "marks a turning point" → Show the effect. Readers will judge the size. Instead of "This release marks a pivotal moment and plays a crucial role in our journey", write "This release halves cold-start time".
- "does not need every", "rather than every" → Say which cases need it and which do not. Instead of "A team does not need every tool on day one", write "Start with CI and error alerts. Add tracing after launch".
- "helps explain why" → Say "explains", or state how much it explains. Instead of "Cost helps explain why few teams adopt it", write "At $40 a seat, most teams pass".
- "rather than treating", "not simply whether" → Say what to do. Skip the straw version. Instead of "Rather than treating errors as failures, the team sees them as signals", write "The team logs each error and reviews the top five every Monday".

While working, drop these agent habits:

- An easier version swapped in for the spec → Stop and say what blocks the real approach.
- "All tests pass" without running them → Quote the command and its output, or say it was not run.
- Part of the job reported as all of it → Count what was done and list what was not.
- Made-up hashes, output and data → Quote only what a tool returned.
- A failed command read as success → Check exit codes and confirm state before the next step.
- Undoing the user's own edits → Work around changes you didn't make, and ask if they block you.

Phrases GPT-4.1 uses far more than human writers (Graphite, 2026): "approach ensures", "stands as", "article explores", "conclusion a", "this article explores", "stands as a", "approach not only", "approach ensures that", "let's explore how", "this approach not".

Prefer: specific nouns and numbers, contractions where speech would use them, one reader in mind, and endings that stop when the information does.

Check with `npx shibbo check <file>`.

eval.data: Graphite AI Tells articles (9,984 topics; human vs. 9 models). Split 50/50 by URL hash.
eval.note: AUC = chance a model article gets a higher penalty than a human article on the same test set. flagged = share scoring below 80. Registry rules were written after viewing Graphite's full-data tell lists, so registry-only numbers are optimistic; the lexicon is rebuilt from the train half only.

source.title: RAID: A Shared Benchmark for Robust Evaluation of Machine-Generated Text Detectors (Dugan et al., ACL 2024)

raid.design: Each model's generations against exactly the human texts they were prompted from (matched by source_id). Attack-free split, sampling without repetition penalty, genres: abstracts, books, news, recipes, reddit, reviews, wiki.

habits.label: Echo ending
habits.what: Share of articles whose last paragraph restates the first

habits.label: Stock AI words
habits.what: Words like crucial, landscape, foster, nuance

habits.label: Call-to-action close
habits.what: Ending on a call to action

habits.label: Hopeful-future close
habits.what: Ending on hope for the future

habits.label: Formula close
habits.what: Ending on a formula such as “in conclusion”

habits.label: Repeated key words
habits.what: Content words used again and again

habits.label: Mixed lists
habits.what: Bullets and numbers mixed in one article

habits.label: Even sentences
habits.what: Spread of sentence lengths (models vary less)

habits.label: Flattery
habits.what: Sycophantic phrases (people use more in these articles)

arena.method: Battles on Graphite's held-out topics (people vs. nine models, same topic). Fewer tell points per 1,000 words wins; ties split. Bradley-Terry ratings on an Elo-like scale (geometric mean 1000); 95% intervals from 200 topic resamples. Checker uses a phrase list built from the train half only.

source.license: MIT (repo LICENSE names Results datasets and slop lists as MIT; js/wordfreq.js is Apache-2.0)

metric.name: Slop Score
metric.description: Composite 0-100: 60% slop-word hits per 1k words, 25% not-x-but-y contrast patterns per 1k chars, 15% slop-trigram hits per 1k words; each part min-max scaled across the leaderboard models (range widened 10% each side), as the eqbench.com page computes it. Recomputed here from the raw metrics with the page formula; raw parts given in `components`. Score is relative to this 23-entry set, so it shifts if models are added. Prompts: creative writing and essays.

source.title: Longform Creative Writing Benchmark results (EQ-bench/longform-writing-bench), results/longform_results_with_metrics.json
source.license: MIT (README: "MIT. Attribution appreciated but not required."); no LICENSE file in repo
source.note: Older snapshot (repo last pushed 2025-10-26), mid-2025 models only. Its scale differs from the live eqbench.com Longform table, which uses newer code and is not extracted here.

metric.name: Longform slop_score
metric.description: Weighted hits of the top 600 entries of data/slop_phrase_prob_adjustments.json per 1,000 words of generated chapters (core/metrics.py calculate_slop_index). Absolute, not min-max scaled.

source.title: The Last Fingerprint: How Markdown Training Shapes LLM Prose (E. M. Freeburg, arXiv:2603.27006v1, 2026-03-27), Table 1
source.license: CC BY 4.0 (arXiv page and repo LICENSE)

metric.name: Em dashes per 1,000 words (unconstrained)
metric.description: Em dash rate in ~10,000 words of essay prose per model with no style instruction. `constrained` is the same rate when the prompt bans markdown. Human baseline 3.23 (mean of 8 published essays, 57,232 words).
metric.direction: higher = more em dashes (not a judgment; human mean is 3.23)
